planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil at a streamside or seep in deep shade, matching its native Klamath-Siskiyou forest-floor habitat.

directions: A monotypic genus found only along streambanks in the Klamath-Siskiyou region of northern California and southern Oregon, this rare saxifrage relative carries rounded, heuchera-like basal leaves and a slender spike of tiny white flowers in late spring. It is a genuine botanical rarity for collectors wanting a true conservation-priority woodland plant, and it needs its roots kept constantly moist in deep shade, failing quickly if the site dries out. Source only nursery-propagated divisions from a specialty native-plant grower given its restricted wild range.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring into moist, gravelly, humus-rich soil at a cool, high-latitude or high-elevation site with reliable summer moisture.

directions: The hardiest boykinia in cultivation, native to Alaska, the Yukon, and far-northern British Columbia along subarctic streambanks and alpine slopes, this species carries large, rounded, deeply cut leaves and a dense spike of pink-tinged white flowers, showier than the more southerly Boykinia species already grown. It needs cool summers and constant soil moisture, performing poorly in hot, humid, or dry climates, so it suits far-northern or high-elevation gardens best. Site it in dappled shade along a stream or seep rather than a conventional dry shade bed.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade under conifer or mixed forest canopy, matching its native montane forest-floor habitat.

directions: A Rocky Mountain and Pacific Northwest montane forest-floor groundcover named for its distinctively three-toothed, fringed petals, this miterwort fills a texture niche among the existing Mitella species with finer, more deeply divided foliage. It spreads slowly by rhizome into a loose mat under conifer or mixed forest canopy and needs consistently moist, cool, humus-rich soil to thrive. It is a good companion for ferns and other small-scale woodland groundcovers rather than a stand-alone specimen.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring into gravelly, consistently wet soil directly alongside a cold stream, seep, or pond margin in dappled shade.

directions: A widespread western mountain saxifrage that grows literally in the splash zone of cold subalpine and alpine streams, this species carries rounded, toothed leaves in a basal rosette and a loose cluster of small white flowers on a reddish stem. It demands constant moisture at its roots and cool summer temperatures, making it best suited to a streamside rock garden or pond-margin planting rather than a typical border. Pair it with other alpine wetland species rather than dry-shade woodland perennials.

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets in spring into gravelly, well-drained but seasonally moist soil tucked into a rock crevice or talus slope in dappled shade.

directions: A Pacific Northwest cliff and talus saxifrage named for the rust-red flecking that often appears on its small white flowers, this species occupies rocky, seasonally wet ledges and crevices rather than the flat forest floor most shade saxifrage relatives prefer. It suits a vertical rock-garden wall or scree slope with dappled shade and reliable winter-spring moisture, going through a drier summer rest once bloom finishes. Give it sharp drainage around the crown even though it wants moisture at the root during the growing season.

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets in fall into moist, open soil in a vernally wet meadow or grassy opening with dappled shade that dries by summer.

directions: A low rosette-forming saxifrage of vernally moist meadows and open woodland edges from British Columbia to California, this species blooms early, often among the first wildflowers up in late winter and early spring, with small white flowers on slender branching stems. It follows a wet-winter, dry-summer cycle typical of western Mediterranean-climate meadows, going dormant once the ground dries rather than needing water year-round. Plant it at a woodland-edge or meadow-garden site that gets good winter moisture but drains by summer.

subcategory: moist cliff and talus shade perennial

planting.note: Divide small rosette offsets in spring into gravelly, humus-flecked soil tucked into a moist rock crevice or talus seep in dappled shade.

directions: A Pacific Northwest cliff and talus specialist with rounded, lobed, buttercup-like leaves, this species complements the already-present Suksdorfia violacea with white rather than violet flowers, giving a color-pair option for a shaded rock garden. It roots naturally into mossy crevices and seepy talus where moisture lingers after snowmelt, so give it a crevice planting with sharp drainage around the crown but steady moisture reaching the roots. It stays small and is best appreciated up close in a trough or crevice garden.
